entries.title: In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak review – what Madame Bovary thought of Flaubert
entries.summary: This audacious portrait of the French author through the eyes of his women is Shafak’s love letter to literature in dark timesIn Frantumaglia, her collection of essays on writing and reading, Elena Ferrante writes that she has sometimes dismissed Gustave Flaubert as a “misogynist”, angered by his invention of as callous a mother as Emma Bovary. entries.content:
In Frantumaglia, her collection of essays on writing and reading, Elena Ferrante writes that she has sometimes dismissed Gustave Flaubert as a “misogynist”, angered by his invention of as callous a mother as Emma Bovary. In other moods, however, she has wondered whether Flaubert allows his female characters to say what “women truly think and say and live but do not dare write”.

Ferrante’s ambivalence is, I think, the most fitting feminist response to Flaubert’s novel. It’s tempting to castigate him as a male writer who kills his female character because he can’t imagine any other end for a transgressive woman; to reproach him for not giving Emma Bovary the profundity of emotion with which Tolstoy imbues Anna Karenina. But this isn’t the whole story, because Flaubert was so complex a figure: restlessly self-doubting even as he more than held his own in an age of cocksure egos; ecstatically happy in his solitary states of aesthetic creation precisely because they could throw him outwards into other people’s stories and minds.

Elif Shafak’s audacious new novel is written out of this ambivalence. An opening chapter shows a devastated Flaubert killing what the narrator styles as “the only woman he has ever loved with heart, mind and soul”, by writing the end of Madame Bovary. The book then shifts briskly to Emma’s own voice, angry with her creator for denying her the freedom to learn from her mistakes (“Could it be because I am a woman?”). These two visions of Flaubert, teeming with creative passion for his own protagonist on the one hand and an exasperating misogynist on the other, become the twin poles of a vast 600-page novel exploring his life from every possible perspective. Thankfully, Shafak doesn’t attempt to ventriloquise Flaubert himself, master of the mot juste. Instead, she has Emma summon the voices of 30 feminine figures, human or otherwise, encountered by Flaubert between birth and death, and alternates their accounts with that of the third-person narrator.

This is the ideal vehicle for Shafak, who delights and often excels in giving voice to anyone and everyone, including, memorably, the tree protagonist in The Island of Missing Trees. I have always admired Shafak’s storytelling verve while not quite falling for her whimsicality, and I balked slightly at the fancifulness of the chapters voiced by Opium (“Let me lighten up your load, ease the burden. I shall cradle you in my warm embrace”) and Syphilis (“I will damage your cells, burrow into your brain, penetrate your dreams”).

But Flaubert himself might have been drawn to these extremes of literary inhabitation, which are a sort of extreme realisation of his own famous statement to Louise Colet: “It is a delicious thing to write. Today, for instance, as man and woman, both lover and mistress, I rode in a forest on an autumn afternoon under the yellow leaves, and I was also the horses, the leaves, the wind.” Certainly, I fell for Jamilah the camel (“I smile all the time. I cannot help it”), who comes at a point when the reader has either thrown the book aside in exasperation or been carried away by its abundance. “I saw those knives – and I smiled”: Shafak imbues Jamilah’s death with genuine tragedy, at a time when the inhabitants of defeated Paris are murdering zoo animals for restaurants to serve up as gourmet dishes.

Throughout, Shafak powerfully evokes the minute-by-minute sensory experience of a sensitive child, and then of the adult still tragically caught up in his childhood world. She is astute and often moving on the main players in Flaubert’s life: the eventually overbearing mother who she suggests couldn’t quite bring herself to love him as an infant after losing several children before him; the sister whose death he never recovered from; the adored niece he allowed to be pushed into an unhappy marriage, despite understanding more profoundly than anyone in his century quite how unhappy such marriages could be; the lover who “thought I could help him, gently peeling off his loneliness like wallpaper lifted from a tired wall”.

It’s with the invented minor characters that Shafak’s gift for storytelling finds its fullest expression. It’s as though she has tunnelled through Flaubert’s refined stylisation back into 19th-century chaos and exuberance, giving us a female murderer whose sister, passing as male, turns up to tutor the unteachable young Gustave; and the wife of the prosecutor who brought Madame Bovary to trial, laughing here at her husband’s secret hobby of writing pornographic poems. . By the end, Shafak’s powers of narrative invention become a kind of bravura performance, as unexpected, splendidly unlikely connections emerge between minor characters and disparate scenes.

In an author’s note Shafak describes the novel as her “love letter to literature”. Certainly she shares Flaubert’s often idealistic sense that literature can help us even when everything else in our lives and world becomes bleak. “Without stories, without art, our descent into savagery would be even swifter,” she has Flaubert just about convincingly muse. Occasionally, I yearned for more of Flaubert’s cold analysis and sheer vitriol alongside the idealism. But this is unashamedly Shafak’s Flaubert, and I am glad of her faith in storytelling as a shaky light guiding us in dark times, even if I can’t always confidently share it.

entries.title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity
entries.summary: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know
entries.content:
‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.”

She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.

When we meet, Winterson is just back from China, where, she tells me, her first novel, Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit, a fictionalised account of her childhood, has sold more than a million copies in the past six years; more than 200,000 mostly young women tried to come to see her speak. She thinks this is because, in a world of long work hours and looming AI-engendered precarity, this fictionalised account of her own escape from an entrapped childhood gives readers permission to imagine a different future for themselves. She has since written 13 novels for adults, as well as nonfiction, short stories, children’s books and screenplays. Now she wants to persuade the production company Goalhanger to give her a podcast. “I want to do one called The Rest is Human,” she says, sitting at a bare wooden table in her home, a Georgian set of rooms above a shop – which she also owns – in Spitalfields, east London. “To see what we retain for ourselves in this absolute scramble to outsource everything we thought we were.”

Because we are, she argues, at a turning point in our story as a species. Until the Industrial Revolution, change was all about “Mother Nature and the slow process of becoming”, but then we “massively intervened. And that’s a decisive moment.” Computing, 70 years ago, was another step. Artificial intelligence – which she would prefer to call alternative intelligence – is next, and “an evolutionary leap. That’s what this is. AI is much more than a tool.” Given this, a certain understanding of the irreducibly human – our feelings, our imaginations, our centuries of study of who we are and what we have done – must be central to how well or badly things might go.

She’s often strikingly optimistic about it. She imagines a relationship with AI, for instance, where you can “have a chat to your system. It’s going to look at everything. It’s going to go at such speed. It’s going to look at transport. It’s going to look at utilities. It’s going to look at employment, going to look at job hours, going to say, ‘What do these weird things called humans thrive on? What do they like? And have they always liked it?’ We could do this in a genuinely utopian way and say, ‘Right, we’re going to make it better.’” We are at a deeply significant moment of choice, she believes, that mirrors the choice we had in the Industrial Revolution – namely, “What future shall we build?”

But in failing to distribute its gains fairly, the Industrial Revolution ushered in an era of unprecedented wealth for the few and unprecedented levels of misery for the many – a state of affairs many predict is not only already echoed but will be dwarfed by the fallout from AI: a permanent underclass, entire continents left behind and starved of current sources of income. Not to mention the environmental impact of datacentres at a time when the world can least afford it.

The problem is not AI, she insists, but us. “There is no inevitable dystopia.” If things go wrong, it will be because of “old-fashioned thinking laid over this brand-new reality”. Specifically, “the idea of meaningless endless work being good for the soul is a 19th-century madness designed to keep people in their place. Most of what we fear about AI and jobs comes down to the political and economic choices our masters will make, just as they did in the Industrial Revolution.” She isn’t blindly optimistic. She does know that, “Yes, we are on track to mess up this chance to fundamentally change our relationship to the world of work” – but that’s because “our masters are using out-of-date, not-fit-for-purpose economic models”.

But it isn’t only the old winner-takes-all, “rational” ends-justify-the-means economic models that are the problem. Our flawed assumptions, and our prejudices, being the material on which large language models (LLMs) are trained, are built into the very fabric of AI. Not to mention the characters and the moral imaginations of those developing it. When we meet, Winterson is reading Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, and reiterates Lepore’s argument that we are now living “the sci-fi books that these [men who are] ruling the world read when they were 13. And she said, ‘We are now all under the covers with these boys and their flashlights. And the thing is, they didn’t read them as warnings about how to preserve what’s good in us. They read them as instruction manuals.’ It’s absolutely terrifying.”

One big thing they seem to have taken from these books, and Winterson cannot help but be fascinated by, is “the ultimate goal of Silicon Valley … to get out of the body and off the planet” – not least because she is so aware that humanism, in which everything is brought back to ourselves, our perceptions and our bodies, is historically so recent. People say, “These are machines, you can’t have relationships with them,” she says. “I look at them and say, ‘billions of people on this Earth right now are having their most profound relationship with a non-biological entity they call their sky god.’ Right? It’s always been so! We are absolutely primed not to worry about biology being everything about us. That’s why religion was invented – it is the world’s first disruptive startup. It’s there to say, this is not it. This is not the end, this doesn’t matter, this is a transition.”

So we’re literally making our own gods? “Totally! What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted,” which is, at its most basic level, a solution to the problem of death. “I mean, has there ever been a time where religion and science are asking the same question, since the Enlightenment? They’re both saying, ‘Is consciousness obliged to materiality?’ And religion has always said no. And science has always said yes. And now science is saying, ‘Um, noooo.”’ You know, to me, where I come from” – a childhood of fundamentalist Christianity in 1960s Accrington, and training as a preacher – “this is completely fascinating.” Later, on email, she adds, “I love my body, but I would be happy to shape shift. Happy to slip out of it into pure consciousness one day and of course people say there is no consciousness without a body, and that was the scientific belief. But now? Haha.”

I would, I have to say, argue the opposite, that advances in neuroscience, immunology and psychotherapy mean it is more the scientific belief than ever. Not to mention the fact that AI is also entirely dependent on a physical system, otherwise known as datacentres. Although, as she points out it’s important to remember that “the machines don’t have a limbic system. They’re only neural networks. But we’ve got two systems – we’re like a hybrid car with two powertrains, so we’ve got the neural network, our rational processing self, and we’ve got the limbic system, which is much older and that’s the fight-flight-freeze, and where all our feelings come from.” Perhaps detaching from the limbic is the next stage, she says, and it definitely isn’t all good. “Maybe we’ll decide that we don’t need this feeling machine … that is where the tech bros are heading. I don’t know if you’ve ever sat in a room with some of these bigger guys, because it’s very interesting. They are not connected to their feelings. They find them kind of bothersome.”

This tech-enabled possibility of a kind of transcendence seems to have arrived alongside a requirement for faith – in the technology, in the future it is making, in the people building that future, in its predictions both of utopian heaven and various shades of hell, all by high priests who jealously guard access to what’s actually going on. “What we know about humans is they love monopolies,” says Winterson, “because it’s a concentration of power. Of course it can be corporatised, monopolised to such a degree that it becomes the worst prison imaginable,” as told in Joanna Kavenna’s brilliant 2019 dystopian novel Zed. “That is a real possibility,” she says. “And that’s why we need people who are sort of free-range humans, who can think.”

The problem then is how we support – or develop – such humans. “There are basically two ways to know you have a future,” claimed Alex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, recently. “One, you have some vocational training. Or two, you’re neurodivergent.” Daniela Amodei, the president of Anthropic and herself a literature graduate, when asked more or less the same thing, had a different take. “I actually think studying the humanities is going to be more important than ever,” she said, because “the things that make us human will become much more important instead of much less important.” Which makes the bonfire of the humanities in the UK somewhat concerning: in the year to December 2024, 4,000 jobs in the social sciences, humanities and arts were lost. Exeter University recently announced it would be cutting 150 roles, affecting eight in 10 academics in the faculty of humanities, arts and social sciences, while last month Nottingham said it would be ending its modern languages and its music degrees. At some universities the humanities, according to a report in this paper, risk being “extinguished” altogether.

Why save the humanities? One answer might be that they teach a sense of where we come from and who we are, which also feels threatened. “Massive numbers of students are going to emerge from university with degrees, and into the workforce, who are essentially illiterate,” one professor told New York magazine, responding to the first tranche of AI natives arriving in higher education. “Both in the literal sense and in the sense of being historically illiterate and having no knowledge of their own culture, much less anyone else’s.” It risked, a report from MIT claimed, being a kind of generational “cognitive surrender”.

Another is the processes by which people should be taught – reading, and being critical of what is read, and then having to write cogent defences of those critiques. Having to tussle your intuitions into an essay helps you to discover what – and how – you think, and how the ideas of others work. Winterson, who studied English at Oxford, and has been professor of new writing at the University of Manchester for 14 years, as well as teaching “a free-thinking class about creativity”, agrees. But she is dismissive of much of the current system. “Maybe I’m controversial here but I do think higher education needs a top-down restructure. I don’t think it’s viable and I don’t think it’s delivering in its present form.” The thing is, “We’ve got a market that doesn’t really know what education is for. Is it for jobs? Is it for personal growth? There are a lot of worthless higher education courses which are not helping, either. I think it’s always better, being a practical northern girl, to face the facts to start with.”

We need to think, she says, about “what’s reserved to us that isn’t going to be done bigger, better, faster, stronger by the machines. And that’s where higher education really comes in. The question that’s sitting on top of all these things about, ‘Why are these jobs going?’, ‘What’s happening in these courses that aren’t getting any applicants any more?’, is ‘What sort of humans will we need in the world to come? What are humans for? What are we going to do with us?’”. And that “takes us back to the idea of, well, OK, how do you develop a mind? How do you protect a mind? Because the mind is this massive, monstrous place where anything can happen.”

And for this, “a humanist education is essential. We have to centre the human here. By changing how we educate our kids from the start we can foreground creativity, play, problem-solving, thinking, because it’s fun to think, the arts because humans are naturally creative. Show me a child that doesn’t want to hear a story or do a dance or paint a picture or have an imaginary friend. This isn’t imposed and it isn’t elitism. It’s us.”

Even an hour a week, she thinks, would make a difference. “Let’s ask what you think about the world. ‘Why do you think that?’ It’s not costly. It’s actually about will.” Teach maths and arts and science, she suggests, at least to A-level, even if they aren’t examined. “Of course we will specialise. We need doctors and chemists but we also need what used to be called well-rounded people. Everything is interesting! Humans are born with a big brain. Mostly we don’t use it.”

Once past formal education, she would embed artists and public intellectuals at every level. “The arts aren’t a leisure industry,” as she puts it in 12 Bytes. “The arts have always been an imaginative and emotional wrestle with reality – a series of inventions and creations. A capacity to think differently, a willingness to change our understanding of ourselves. To help us to be wiser, more reflective, less frightened people. Artists make something out of nothing every day.”

We meet before Jacob Coxon quit his job at Anthropic to warn of a 10% chance AI might erase humanity, sending a wave of panic across the world. Afterwards, I check in about how positive Winterson is feeling now. The worst “could happen”, she repeats. But “the immensity of the good outcome is just as real as the totality of our failure to get this right”. Above all, “this is a human decision and a human predicament. This is our big chance. Maybe our last chance, just like Turing’s colleague Jack Good said when he called AI our last invention. It’s all to play for.”

We can only hope it’s not too late.

Jeanette Winterson’s most recent book is One Aladdin, Two Lamps. She also writes at jeanettewinterson.substack.com

  • One Aladdin Two Lamps by Jeanette Winterson (Vintage Publishing, £12.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy for £10.39 at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? by Judi Dench review – whatever you do, don’t call her a ‘national treasure’
entries.summary: The actor waxes lyrical on directors, dildos and why she hates being referred to as though she’s a dusty old relicIn the late 1950s, Judi Dench was invited to meet a major Hollywood producer about a possible career in the film business. The producer looked at her for a long time and said: “Very nice to meet you but you’ll never make a movie because you have every single thing wrong with your face.
entries.content:
In the late 1950s, Judi Dench was invited to meet a major Hollywood producer about a possible career in the film business. The producer looked at her for a long time and said: “Very nice to meet you but you’ll never make a movie because you have every single thing wrong with your face.” As she left his office, Dench – who was 23 and about to make her professional debut as Ophelia in Hamlet at the Old Vic – breathed a sigh of relief and resolved to concentrate on theatre. Though she dabbled in film and TV, it wasn’t until the 1990s that she became a bona fide movie star, playing M in the Bond films and winning an Oscar for her portrayal of Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love. Yet, she notes: “Being onstage is where I feel safest. Yes, I’ve appeared in films, but I’d never consider myself a film actor.”

Dench’s reflections on her working life form the backbone of Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?, a memoir built around her conversations with the actor and theatre director Brendan O’Hea, Dench’s friend with whom she also collaborated on 2023’s Shakespeare: The Man Who Pays the Rent. This book confirms much of what is already known about Dench: that she is impishly funny, swears like a sailor, and that, despite that film producer’s unkind comments, she has “no hang-ups about what I look like on camera … Acting for me is not about looking glamorous. It’s whatever’s needed for the story.” We also learn that Dench, who is 91, can’t resist a prank: while playing Brecht’s Mother Courage at the Barbican in London, she replaced the drinks her character serves to two soldiers with cider vinegar – “It was a joy watching them knock it back, made even more glorious by the fact they had to ask for a top-up.”

In keeping with her previous book, this one is delivered in a question-and‑answer format. The chapters are thematic and cover faith, animals, directors and directing, comedy, choosing a part, which means the chronology is all over the place. While the book starts quite reasonably with Dench’s early life in York as the daughter of a GP, it ends, oddly, with a chapter called Starting Out, in which we learn what she did after her A-levels. And while she has an easy chemistry with O’Hea, there are times when his line of questioning gets tediously granular, as in: “What’s your favourite dressing room?” Such are the perils of having an actor interview an actor.

But despite the shoptalk and the haphazard structure, there are enough witty anecdotes and oddball facts to keep it clipping along. We learn that Dench has a waste-collection truck named after her: “Dame Foodie Dench”; that she had a cat called Bernard the Duck Fucker (though O’Hea neglects to ask how he earned his name); and that, on the opening night of Madame de Sade, Dench’s co-star Frances Barber gave her a double-ended, bendy dildo which she wore as a scarf when the company gathered for director’s notes. Elsewhere, Dench pays touching tribute to departed friends including the late Maggie Smith, whom she says was “a very complex person – intensely private, and I suspect quite lonely at times; she’d occasionally erect an electric fence around herself”.

The whole project is kept afloat by Dench’s rare humour and warmth which long ago elevated her to national treasure status (an appellation she loathes as it makes her sound “like a dusty old relic”). Her eyesight is now poor, but her memories are pin-sharp, relayed through a prism of amused self-deprecation and passion for her job. The book’s title references Dench’s professional nerves, which lead her to keep her bag by the rehearsal room door in case she is compelled to do a runner. Learning lines may have become more difficult, but she has no intention of stopping work. “Take the keys out of the ignition and the car will conk out,” she cautions. “Don’t retire, do not go gentle, and don’t even think about going quietly.”

entries.title: Michael Gambon: the authorised biography review – a brilliant actor, and a master deceiver
entries.summary: From the National Theatre to Harry Potter, Gambon’s shapeshifting life leaves many questions still unansweredMichael Gambon began his acting career with a preposterous bluff. Applying for a job at Dublin’s Gate theatre, the young toolmaker from the south-east London suburbs embellished his CV with entirely fabricated theatrical experience. It was a gamble, but it worked. In 1962 he made his profes
entries.content:
Michael Gambon began his acting career with a preposterous bluff. Applying for a job at Dublin’s Gate theatre, the young toolmaker from the south-east London suburbs embellished his CV with entirely fabricated theatrical experience. It was a gamble, but it worked. In 1962 he made his professional debut as the Second Gentleman in Othello. The following year he was hired by Laurence Olivier for the brand new National Theatre.

Gambon carried on telling tall tales long after there was any need. Some were self-aggrandising: he had been a dancer with the Royal Ballet, worked as a nuclear physicist and auditioned for James Bond. To be fair, this last one was half-true – producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli had once called him in for a chat. Others were absurdities for the sake of it: he was thinking of buying a house in Hanoi, his mother had operated cranes in Dublin. Occasionally, the lies were intended to save his skin. Terrified of being sacked for turning up late yet again to rehearsal at the National, he claimed that his mother had died in the night. She went on to live for another 49 years. More often, he lied to make other people laugh, claiming that he had worked with the Russian director Dmitri Shagyerarsoff.

Gambon’s compulsion to invent and conceal presents obvious challenges for Jasper Rees, the veteran stage and showbiz journalist who interviewed the actor several times before his death in 2023 and reports always coming away feeling puzzled. Rees’s authorised biography draws on the archive held by Gambon’s wife, Anne, a woman whose existence was unknown to most of his colleagues. For years Gambon had a relationship with the National Theatre administrator Lyn Haill and was later photographed with set designer Philippa Hart, with whom he had two sons. Yet, apart from a brief period in the early 1970s, he remained in the marital home in Kent. That marriage lasted 61 years, and Anne and their son Fergus accompanied Gambon to Buckingham Palace when he was knighted in 1998.

Rees largely leaves his subject’s private life tactfully alone, focusing instead on the origins of Gambon’s talent for deflecting scrutiny. He belonged to no obvious cohort or peer group. Unlike Tom Courtenay and Albert Finney, he had not attended drama school. Unlike Ian McKellen and Derek Jacobi, he had not made his way to Cambridge on a scholarship. Instead he emerged from working-class London-Irish amateur dramatics, where his practical skills were useful for building sets. This delight in making and tinkering remained with him throughout his life: in his home workshop he once built an exact replica of an antique pistol that he’d been asked to restore by a West End dealer, “so really I’m a faker”.

Rees cross-references Gambon’s tall tales with other actors’ archives and draws on more than 100 new interviews, including conversations with Eileen Atkins, Penelope Wilton, Brian Cox and Simon Russell Beale. He also uses the archive of New York Times critic Mel Gussow, whose collection of interviews with Gambon appeared in 2004. The result is probably as near as anyone will get to a definitive account of Gambon’s life and career, although you would not want to bet on one or two of the actor’s misdirections slipping through undetected.

Despite being chosen by Olivier for the nascent National, Gambon initially failed to progress much beyond spear-carrying. His thuggish good looks – he was over 6ft tall, barrel-built, with a face of fleshy menace – made him useful as background colour. His unfamiliarity with the classical and modern repertory, not to mention the demands of iambic pentameter, left him ill-equipped for more demanding roles. Only after leaving in 1967 in search of better parts did his potential emerge. Most notably he played Tom in the London opening of Alan Ayckbourn’s The Norman Conquests.

Gambon’s return to the National in 1978 saw him triumph in Pinter’s new play Betrayal and a revival of Brecht’s The Life of Galileo, which established him as a leading stage actor. In 1986, his performance in the BBC’s The Singing Detective made him a household name. Although he was reportedly not the first choice, the part of Dennis Potter’s Philip Marlow could have been written for him. Confined to a hospital bed by psoriatic arthritis and heavily bandaged, Marlow escapes his anguish by imagining parallel lives. He becomes a private detective and nightclub crooner, inhabiting a world of femmes fatales and Nazi spies, while revisiting a childhood scarred by his parents’ sexual unhappiness. Gambon plays a man who assumes multiple identities but never escapes himself.

He liked to give the impression that he never planned anything, simply accepting the next job that came up. Perhaps that was true: there were certainly some poor choices along the way. For the moment, though, Gambon made the most of his newfound stardom. The following year, he played Eddie Carbone in Arthur Miller’s A View from the Bridge. Miller was enchanted: “This guy can really disappear into a role.” The Guardian wrote that it showed “Michael Gambon shaking hands with greatness”.

Rees devotes perhaps too much of this nearly 600-page book to Gambon’s mischief on stage and screen. His interviewees recall fart machines, water bombs and ad libs designed to throw fellow actors off their lines. The stories are often funny, but their cumulative effect is less comfortable. Was Gambon merely an antic fool, or was he a bit of a sadist? Rees leaves the verdict to his witnesses. Penelope Wilton recalls that the water pistols “got very tedious”.

During RSC rehearsals Eileen Atkins remembers him saying, “I don’t bother with matinees, I just say the words”, which made her furious. He also lost interest once a production had peaked. After the triumphant opening of A View from the Bridge, he began, says co-star Michael Simkins, to “gently destroy it”. His performances deteriorated and the anticipated New York transfer never materialised.

Gambon’s gradual decline makes for painful reading. In his late 50s he began to struggle with lines, flubbing them or improvising in ways that were no longer funny. Prompt boards were introduced, followed by “earwigs”, tiny earpieces through which a prompter fed him lines. This worked best on screen, where performances could be patched together from multiple takes, as happened in the Harry Potter films, where Gambon took over as Dumbledore after Richard Harris’s death. On stage, the difficulties became increasingly hard to conceal. Rees reveals that Gambon was diagnosed with dementia, something which he always denied, perhaps because he had watched his mother ravaged by the disease. It is at this late stage that we begin to glimpse the vulnerability and terror of exposure that lay beneath decades of blustery bravado.

Rees avoids a conventional cradle-to-grave structure by following each main chapter with an interlude devoted to an aspect of Gambon’s character or career that might otherwise get lost in the narrative. One explores his beautifully elegant hands, evident in his wand work in Harry Potter; another his love of fast cars, memorably displayed on Top Gear’s Star in a Reasonably Priced Car segment, when he almost overturned a family saloon.

Rees’s chief challenge is to convey what made Gambon such a great actor. He collates the testimony of colleagues and the verdicts of critics, but neither quite captures the alchemy of a performance. Nor can the actor’s wildly conflicting qualities be assembled into a single coherent character. This unresolved tension is not a failure of the biography so much as its most fitting conclusion: one suspects it is exactly the way that Gambon would have liked it.

entries.title: Time Being by Jude Cook review – a smart existential tale of midlife
entries.summary: A fatal mistake sparks this juicy melodrama, in which a philosophy professor navigates the guilt of being a survivorWhat if, battered by cancer and cancer treatment, you decided to end your life? And what if it went wrong and you lived, but a friend died in your place? Would you tell the police the truth? Or reason that there’s no point punishing your grieving, bruised self any further, especially
entries.content:
What if, battered by cancer and cancer treatment, you decided to end your life? And what if it went wrong and you lived, but a friend died in your place? Would you tell the police the truth? Or reason that there’s no point punishing your grieving, bruised self any further, especially when – in the first bit of good news you’ve had for years – you learn that your treatment may finally be working?

It’s the kind of moral question that London philosophy professor Esther Luck loves throwing at her students. But Jude Cook’s third novel makes the dilemma bracingly personal. As it opens, Esther, who has ovarian cancer, is waiting in a toilet cubicle on the fifth floor of her university building – the only one without CCTV – for the arrival of her dodgy French ex, Michel. He has agreed to shoot through the door and end her misery. But someone else arrives first. Laura is the department’s fragrant superstar, with her BBC presenting gig and handsome barrister husband. She finds an empty stall, Michel gets the wrong door, and Esther is left guilty, panicked and alone on the loo as Laura’s blood pools on the floor.

The setup may feel like a Tarantino subplot, but Cook is here less for the violent drama than the existential questions that follow. His debut, Byron Easy, saw a poet mull over his frustrated life on a train, while its successor, Jacob’s Advice, followed two cousins as they discussed Europe, identity and terrorism. True to form, Time Being does not take long to hunker down with Esther’s thoughts.

Having given a lecture on autopilot and deflected police questions, she sits in her Crouch End flat and walks in the nearby park, alone with her guilt and sorrow. Steroids have left her heavy and listless; radiotherapy has given her permanent nerve damage and agonising cystitis. She is crushed by her menopause and has few friends. Her career once offered fulfilment and security; now the philosophy department faces savage cuts, and an academic who can barely function is right in the firing line.

But the police investigation seems to be going nowhere fast, and chinks of light appear in Esther’s purgatory: good news from her doctor, an unexpected romance, a chance of a book deal. Esther finds herself hammering out Every Grain of Sand, an introduction to philosophy that’s also a memoir. It is, says her agent, “a book I just know women will identify with”. And for all her misery, Esther’s eye for the world is wonderfully vivid throughout. The new year finds “spring crouching under the churned soil”, while on a rare holiday to a country house hotel, Esther opens her eyes to the stars and basks in the universe.

Yet nothing is entirely untainted. One October morning, she visits her mother’s grave under “a blaze of majestic bronze and apricot” foliage to find freshly painted swastikas on the stones of the Jewish cemetery. The police may seem no closer to solving Laura’s murder, but they return every few months to ask leading questions and sit thoughtfully in Esther’s book-lined office. And can the wild, charismatic Michel simply have vanished?

Like any good philosopher, Esther ponders it all: is life “just one damn thing after another”; is she a “temporal husk of flesh, or something else”? She turns to Boethius, Kant, Arendt, Weil and De Beauvoir, but finds little solace. Indeed, Time Being’s philosophical asides end up feeling like its flimsiest part. The rest of the book is better and more focused, and while the juicy melodrama of Laura’s murder and the bleak mundanity of an unhappy life may seem an uncomfortable marriage, Cook ultimately brings his strands together with confidence.

Throughout, it’s the details and feelings that power Time Being: the heavy silence of the clinic’s waiting room, the happy buzz of an unexpected date, the practised rhythm of a lecture. Esther is a fine and acutely observed creation, at times thoroughly sympathetic, at others grimly evasive, and all the more credible for it: you don’t have to like her to share her dread at the trauma she endures and the brutal decisions she faces. The result is a fine portrait of a wounded midlife, as seasons shift and hope and happiness roll by, glorious but fleeting, like clouds in a turbulent sky.

entries.title: Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li review – a virtuosic interrogation of the power of art
entries.summary: What does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality? Li examines the gulf between talent and genius through the marriage of two real-life musiciansIn his recently published A History of the Novel in Britain, Philip Hensher makes a bold claim. entries.content:
In his recently published A History of the Novel in Britain, Philip Hensher makes a bold claim. Historical novels, he tells us, don’t last. However popular and prestigious a historical novel might be in its day, it will almost always get thrown overboard as the ship of literary culture sails on, piled high with novels of contemporary life. He might be on to something. Who now prefers Walter Scott to Jane Austen? The historical novel risks a double obsolescence, courting a future in which it has become an old-fashioned vision of an old-fashioned time.

However much this news might dismay writers of historical novels, Hensher is untroubled: “As readers enjoying our contemporaries, we should not let our readerly pleasures be affected by the probability of ultimate oblivion.” Will the future, what there is of it, rate Wolf Hall as highly as we do? It doesn’t matter. Posterity, as Gore Vidal once wrote, is “a permanent darkness where no whistle sounds”. What matters is us, now, what we make of history and of our lives – in our novels and elsewhere.

Posterity and its ironies form a central theme of Yiyun Li’s new historical novel. In several senses Music Against the Night isn’t, in fact, “a historical novel” – certainly not in the supermarket-own-brand sense of a cosplay adventure in which affable protagonists find themselves chatting with Byron or whoever. Readers of Li will already know that she soars far above the well-meant strivings of lesser writers, occupying a luminous realm of her own. She has the craft that makes craft invisible, and the art that makes art itself her obsessive subject. In Music Against the Night the art is music, as perceived through the lives, and the real and hoped-for afterlives, of two musicians.

Real musicians, as it happens: a married couple, bound by a “contrapuntal fate”. The pianist and composer John Field, born in Dublin in 1782, is now remembered as the inventor of the nocturne, the form perfected by Chopin. There is a room in the National Concert Hall in Dublin called The Field Room. But to listen to Field’s nocturnes when you know Chopin’s is to ponder the gulf between talent and genius. In Li’s telling, Field himself compulsively ponders this gulf, as he becomes “a footnote in the life of Frédéric Chopin”. Li knows that footnote status is the fate of most artists. What does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality?

In 1807 Field, by then living in Moscow, took on a student named Adelaide Percheron, an orphan raised by her grandmother in Pondicherry, French India. Adelaide too was a gifted musician, but her ambition was thwarted by the patriarchal strictures of the society into which she was born. John and Adelaide (she was known as “Percherette”), separately wrestling with the enemies of promise, married in 1810. It was not an auspicious union.

The ordinary historical novelist starts there, and labours through the tempestuous marriage: Field’s drinking, his affairs, Percherette’s despair. But Li’s subject isn’t marriage. Music Against the Night is about the relationship between life and art; about what it means to sacrifice a life to art; and about what exactly is sacrificed, when such a sacrifice is made. Field and Percherette’s marriage is given to us in brief Muriel Spark-like flash-forwards. Long sections, split between Dublin and Pondicherry, follow Field and Percherette closely through late childhood and early adolescence; this is the bulk of the book. Childhood, for both, is short. Both are prodigies: Field on the pianoforte, Percherette as a kind of psychologist, perceiving the hidden truths of human behaviour. What they share is a “willingness to be rescued from an ordinary childhood”.

Li’s narration is unapologetically omniscient, but she has no use for pastiche: she acknowledges she is writing in the 2020s, and yet there’s no historical-novel clutter about horses or furniture. Only that which impinges on her characters, or her theme, is noted. Her narrator is insistently aphoristic: “To be known is the desire that drives much of the world’s progress, also much of its destruction. History is a discourse against obscurity.” Not all the aphorisms work: “an absent anchor only further disturbs an unmoored heart”. But many of them are superb: “Talent, vision, luck, work – all are necessary for a career, but not sufficient. An artist falls short if he cannot master the art of indifference.”

Engaged in their separate discourses against obscurity, John and Percherette fail to master the art of indifference. Their passionate self-scourgings form a counterpoint to the eerily calm and patient gathering-in effects of Li’s prose. The result is pure readerly pleasure – posterity (and this might be what Li, in this novel of half-forgotten artists, is suggesting) be damned.

Late in the novel there is a brief reflection on the loss of a child. Li herself, of course, has written about the loss of her two sons, Vincent and James, to suicide. The subject is not dwelt on at length in Music Against the Night. It forms merely part of a piercing argument about the passions of life versus the austere and indifferent values of art. The aphoristic narrator remarks: “Death is a subject that rewards minor artists.” But “Life? It requires major talent to convey that.” Li conveys life without apparent effort. Major is the word.
